mainTopic: The end of כלאים in animals, then when and what a hired worker may eat from the produce he works on, including whether he may eat from a different vine.
overview: The amud opens by finishing the topic of כלאים in animals. A ברייתא shows that only mixing different species is forbidden, and that 'holding' an animal of the same species really means inserting, said politely. רב אשי tells how he forbade putting mixed animals in one pen for the house of the ריש גלותא, only because of their slaves. Then a new משנה teaches that a worker may eat even if he works with just his hands, feet or shoulder. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה requires both hands and feet, learning from the threshing ox. Whether birds that thresh would count for him is left as תיקו. Another משנה limits the worker to the same kind of fruit, eaten during work, with extra allowances to save the owner's time. The גמרא then asks whether a worker on one vine may eat from another vine, and tries several proofs from the משנה, each pushed off. In the second version, the last rejection continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A ברייתא explains why the פסוק says 'diverse kinds'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says that without the word 'כלאים,' we would have thought even holding an animal for its own species is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the Torah had only said 'Do not mate your animal,' I would have thought a person may not even hold a female animal so a male can mount her. That is why the פסוק adds 'diverse kinds.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that reads the פסוק carefully to show exactly what the Torah forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'בהמתך לא תרביע' alone could sound like any helping with animal mating is banned. The extra word 'כלאים' narrows the ban to mixing different species only.

keyTerms.meaning: Forbidden mixtures; here, mating two different species of animals
Therefore the פסוק says (introduces the word that teaches the point)

phrases.english: Had it said only: "You shall not let your animal mate"
I would have said:
a person may not hold the animal
so that a male can mount it,
therefore the verse says: "diverse kinds."

steps.triggerLanguage: אִלּוּ נֶאֱמַר ״בְּהֶמְתְּךָ לֹא תַרְבִּיעַ״ הָיִיתִי אוֹמֵר
steps.raayaObject: Whether helping animals of the same species mate is allowed
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading the word 'כלאים' in ויקרא 19:19

steps.title: Inference: the same species is allowed
steps.stepSummary: From the ברייתא we learn that only mixed species are forbidden, so the same species is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Only mixing different kinds is forbidden. So an animal with its own kind is allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the plain lesson from the ברייתא: mating an animal with its own species is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the Torah said 'כלאים,' the ban is tied to different species. The opposite case, מין במינו, falls outside the ban.

keyTerms.meaning: A species with its own species

phrases.english: It is diverse kinds that is forbidden,
but a species with its own species is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּלְאַיִם הוּא דְּאָסוּר, הָא מִין בְּמִינוֹ שְׁרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical lesson from the ברייתא in step 1.

steps.title: Maybe only holding is allowed, not inserting
steps.stepSummary: An attempt to read the ברייתא narrowly: even with the same species, only holding is allowed, not inserting.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even with the same species, maybe holding is allowed but inserting is not!
steps.whatsHappening: Someone pushes back: the ברייתא only spoke about holding the animal, so maybe inserting is still forbidden even with the same species.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא used the word 'יאחוז' (hold). That word choice could suggest that only holding is allowed, while directly guiding the male into the female, even of the same kind, stays forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Inserting; directly guiding the male into the female

phrases.english: And even a species with its own species:
holding, yes; inserting, no!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִין בְּמִינוֹ נָמֵי: אֲחִיזָה אִין, הַכְנָסָה לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how broad the permission in step 2 really is.
steps.kashyaTarget: The full permission of מין במינו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא only mentions holding, which suggests inserting is still forbidden.

steps.title: 'Holding' is a polite word for inserting
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the narrow reading: 'holding' really means inserting, said in clean language.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'holding' mean? Inserting. So why call it 'holding'? Because that is the refined way to say it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא really did mean inserting. It just used a more modest word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אחיזה' is not a limit on what is allowed. It is a לישנא מעליא, a polite way to describe an intimate act. So inserting is also permitted for the same species.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the ברייתא is drawing a line between holding and inserting. 'Holding' is just a modest word, and it really means inserting.

phrases.english: What is "holding"? Inserting.
And why does it call it "holding"?
It is refined language.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״אֲחִיזָה״ הַכְנָסָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the narrow reading in step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Fully rejects the inference that inserting is forbidden for the same species
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The word 'אחיזה' was taken literally, but it is only a polite word for inserting.
steps.whatToRemember: With the same species, both holding and inserting are permitted. Only כלאים, mixing different species, is forbidden.

steps.title: Putting mixed animals together in one pen
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי tells that the house of רב נחמיה ריש גלותא asked him whether three animals, two of one kind and one of another, may be put into one pen.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The people of רב נחמיה the ריש גלותא's house asked me this: may you put an animal, another of its own kind, and one of a different kind into one pen? Since its own kind is there, will it go after its own kind? Or maybe even so it is not allowed?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי reports a practical question about keeping different species together when an animal of the same species is also in the pen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The side for allowing it says the animal will naturally go to its own kind, so crossbreeding will not happen. The side against says there is still a risk of mixed mating, so it should not be done.

keyTerms.meaning: The Exilarch, leader of Babylonian Jewry

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
This matter they asked of me,
the people of the house of Rav Nechemya the Exilarch:
What is the law about bringing in an animal of one species and one of its own species
and one not of its species into the pen?
Since its own species is there,
it is drawn after its own species.
Or perhaps even so, it is not allowed?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא מִילְּתָא בְּעוֹ מִינַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from mating to a related practical case: keeping different species in one pen.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is it allowed to put two animals of one species and one of another species into one pen?

steps.title: רב אשי forbade it because of the slaves
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי ruled it forbidden, even though that is not the halacha, because the slaves of that house were immoral.
steps.simpleTranslation: I answered them that it is forbidden, which is not the real halacha, because of the immoral behavior of the slaves.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives his answer: forbidden. He openly admits the real halacha is lenient, but he was strict for that household.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic law allows it, since the animal goes after its own kind. But רב אשי worried the slaves there would cause mixed mating on purpose and blame it on the animals, so he made a fence just for them.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a רב can rule strictly for a specific place to prevent misuse, while openly saying the real halacha is lenient.

phrases.english: And I resolved it for them as forbidden,
not according to the halacha,
because of the immorality of the slaves.
phrases.notes: He means the servants of that house, who might cause mixed mating on purpose.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפְשַׁטִי לְהוּ לְאִיסּוּרָא דְּלָא כְּהִלְכְתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Forbidden for that house only, because of the slaves; the real halacha permits it.
steps.whatToRemember: The real halacha allows it, because the animal goes after its own kind. רב אשי was strict only because of that household's slaves.

steps.title: New משנה: a worker eats even if he works with only part of his body
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a worker may eat from the produce whether he works with his hands, his feet, or even just his shoulder.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a worker was working with his hands but not his feet, or his feet but not his hands, or even only with his shoulder, he may eat.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins, going back to the topic of a worker eating from the produce he works on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא does not need the worker to use his whole body. Any real work on the produce, even with one part of the body, gives him the right to eat.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: If he was working with his hands
but not with his feet,
or with his feet but not with his hands,
or even only with his shoulder,
this one may eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הָיָה עוֹשֶׂה בְּיָדָיו אֲבָל לֹא בְּרַגְלָיו
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker may eat even if he works with only his hands, only his feet, or only his shoulder.

steps.title: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה: only with hands and feet
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה disagrees: the worker may eat only if he works with both his hands and his feet.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה says: he may not eat until he works with his hands and his feet.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion in the משנה argues with the first and makes the requirement stricter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה, partial work is not enough. The worker must use both hands and feet to earn the right to eat.
steps.whatToRemember: There is a מחלוקת: the תנא קמא lets a worker eat even with partial body work, and רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה requires both hands and feet.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, says:
Not unless he works with his hands and with his feet.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָדָיו וּבְרַגְלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the תנא קמא in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker eats only if he works with both hands and feet.

steps.title: What is the source for the first opinion?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking for the reason behind the תנא קמא's ruling that any kind of work lets a worker eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its discussion of the משנה by asking for the source of the first opinion, that a worker may eat whether he works with his hands, his feet or his shoulder. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave a broad rule without a reason. The גמרא wants to know where in the תורה this broad rule comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה
What is the reason or source?

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He is asking about the first opinion in the משנה, that any kind of work counts.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the ruling stated in step 7
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the view that any kind of work lets a worker eat

steps.title: The verse does not name a specific kind of work
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'כי תבא בכרם רעך' does not limit the kind of work, so any work the worker does counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says, 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard.' This means any work that he does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק speaks generally about coming into a vineyard to work. It does not specify which body part he must use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק names no particular task, so the תנא קמא reads it to include every kind of work. That is why working with only the hands, the feet or even the shoulder is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard,' the פסוק that lets a worker eat

phrases.english: "When you come into your neighbor's vineyard,"
with whatever work he does.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי תָבֹא בְּכֶרֶם רֵעֶךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The general wording of the פסוק includes every kind of work

steps.title: What is the source for רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה's view that a worker needs both hands and feet, and asks for his reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה says: Only once he works with his hands and his feet. What is the reason of רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the second opinion of the משנה so it can ask for its source. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה requires more than the תנא קמא does. The גמרא wants to know what pushes him to demand both hands and feet.

keyTerms.meaning: With his hands and his feet

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says:
Not until he works with his hands and his feet.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה?
phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first opinion's source to the second opinion's source
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה requires work with both hands and feet

steps.title: The worker is compared to the threshing ox
steps.stepSummary: Just as the threshing ox works with its 'hands and feet,' a worker eats only when he works with his hands and feet.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like an ox. Just as an ox eats only when it works with its hands and its feet, so too a worker eats only when he works with his hands and his feet.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה compares the worker to the threshing ox. The ox uses all four legs, so the worker must use both his hands and his feet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law that the worker may eat is linked to the law that the threshing ox may eat. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה copies the ox's way of working into the worker's rule. The תנא קמא instead reads the vineyard פסוק broadly.

keyTerms.meaning: Like an ox, meaning the worker's law follows the threshing ox
Just as... so too; a comparison formula

steps.confusionAlert: An ox has no real 'hands.' Its 'hands' are its front legs and its 'feet' are its back legs, so it threshes with all four.

phrases.english: It is like an ox:

phrases.aramaic: מָה שׁוֹר עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָדָיו וּבְרַגְלָיו –
phrases.english: just as an ox eats only when it works with its hands and its feet,

phrases.aramaic: אַף פּוֹעֵל עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָדָיו וּבְרַגְלָיו.
phrases.english: so too a worker eats only when he works with his hands and his feet.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי שׁוֹר, מָה שׁוֹר עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָדָיו וּבְרַגְלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 11
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A comparison to the threshing ox, which works with all four limbs
steps.whyThisMatters: This comparison is the basis for the next question, about animals that do not have four legs.

steps.title: Threshing with geese and chickens
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא asks how רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה would rule about birds used for threshing: is the point full effort, or literally using four limbs?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא asked: If someone threshed with geese and chickens, what is the law according to רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה? Do we need it to work with all its strength, and that is the case here? Or perhaps we need it to work with hands and feet, and that is not the case here?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב הונא asks what רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה's 'hands and feet' rule means for birds, which have only two legs. He lays out both sides of the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'hands and feet' just means working with full strength, then birds count, because they thresh with all they have. If it literally means four limbs, birds do not count.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked; it introduces a question that needs to be decided
Or perhaps; it introduces the other side of the question

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna asked:
If one threshed with geese and chickens,
what is the law according to Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda?
Do we require it to work with all its strength? That is present here.
Or perhaps we require it to work with its hands and its feet?
That is not present here.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the ox comparison from step 12 on a new case
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה's requirement means full effort or literally four limbs

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finds no answer, and the question about geese and chickens is left standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the discussion without deciding the question about threshing with birds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source settles whether the rule is about full strength or about four limbs. So the question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question remains unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: The תנא קמא learns from the vineyard פסוק that any work counts. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה learns from the ox that hands and feet are needed. Whether birds count according to him is left unresolved (תיקו).

phrases.english: Let it stand unresolved.

steps.triggerLanguage: תֵּיקוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question of step 13 without an answer
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The question of threshing with birds according to רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה remains unresolved

steps.title: When winepress workers may drink wine
steps.stepSummary: Before treading the grapes lengthwise and crosswise, workers may eat grapes but not drink wine. After that, they may do both.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: Before workers have walked lengthwise and crosswise in the winepress, they may eat grapes but may not drink wine. Once they have walked lengthwise and crosswise in the winepress, they may eat grapes and drink wine.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן, quoting רבה בר אבוה, gives a new rule about workers treading grapes. It tells us at what point they may also drink the wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A worker eats from what he is working on. Before the full treading, he is working on grapes, so he may eat only grapes. After treading lengthwise and crosswise, he is working on wine too, so he may drink wine as well.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said that Rabba bar Avuh said:
Workers, before they have walked
lengthwise and crosswise in the winepress,
may eat grapes but may not drink wine.
Once they have walked lengthwise and crosswise in the winepress,
they may eat grapes and drink wine.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new rule about what workers may eat during a specific stage of work
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Workers in the winepress may drink wine only after they have trodden lengthwise and crosswise. Before that, they may eat only grapes.

steps.title: A worker eats only the kind of fruit he works with
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a worker on figs may not eat grapes, and a worker on grapes may not eat figs. He may hold off eating until he reaches better fruit of the same kind.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If he was working with figs, he may not eat grapes. If he was working with grapes, he may not eat figs. But he may hold himself back until he reaches a place with good ones, and then eat.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It limits the worker to eating the same kind of fruit he is working on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker's right to eat is tied to the job he is doing right now, so fruit he is not working on is off-limits. He does not have to eat the very first fruit in front of him. He may wait for nicer fruit, as long as it is the same kind.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין: here begins the משנה

phrases.english: MISHNA: If he was working with figs
he may not eat grapes.
If he was working with grapes, he may not eat figs.
But he may hold himself back
until he reaches a place of good ones, and then eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה עוֹשֶׂה בִּתְאֵנִים לֹא יֹאכַל בַּעֲנָבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the earlier discussion of workers eating grapes and wine.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker may eat only the type of produce he is working with, but he may wait to eat better fruit of that type.

steps.title: Eating only during work, with special allowances to save time
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says all these eating rights apply only during work. To protect the owner's time, the חכמים also let workers eat while walking between rows, when coming back from the winepress, and with a donkey while it is being unloaded.
steps.simpleTranslation: And in all these cases, they said he may eat only at the time of work. But because of returning lost property to the owners, they said: workers may eat as they walk from row to row, and on their way back from the winepress. And with a donkey, it may eat when it is being unloaded.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה sets a time limit: eating is only during work. Then it gives exceptions that actually help the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the right to eat exists only while the worker is working. But if workers stopped work to sit and eat, the owner would lose work time. So the חכמים let them eat during the in-between moments, like walking between rows. That is why the משנה calls it השב אבידה.

keyTerms.meaning: Returning lost property; here, saving the owner's lost work time

steps.whatToRemember: The worker's right to eat is tied to his work: the same kind of produce, and during work time. The חכמים stretched the time rule so workers would not stop working just to eat.

phrases.english: And with regard to all of these, they said
only at the time of work.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מִשּׁוּם הָשֵׁב אֲבֵידָה לַבְּעָלִים אָמְרוּ:
phrases.english: But because of returning lost property to the owners, they said:
phrases.notes: The "lost property" is the owner's work time. If workers stopped to eat, that time would be lost to him.

phrases.english: workers may eat as they walk from row to row,
and on their way back from the winepress,
and with a donkey, when it is being unloaded.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכוּלָּן לֹא אָמְרוּ אֶלָּא בִּשְׁעַת מְלָאכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה, moving from which produce he may eat to when he may eat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating is permitted only during work, but to save the owner's time, workers may eat while walking between rows and returning from the winepress, and a donkey may eat while being unloaded.

steps.title: May a worker on one vine eat from another vine?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a worker on one vine may eat from a different vine. Is the requirement only the same type of produce, or the exact produce he is putting into the owner's vessels?
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: A question was asked: one who is working on this vine, may he eat from another vine? Do we require that it be from the same type that you put into the owner's vessels, and that is true here? Or perhaps we require that it be from the very fruit that you put into the owner's vessels, and that is not true here?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question that grows out of the משנה. Figs and grapes are clearly different, but what about two vines of the same grapes?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to understand the worker's right. If it only has to be the same kind of produce, another vine is fine. If it has to be the actual fruit he is handling for the owner, a different vine is not allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked of them (an open question)

phrases.english: GEMARA: A question was asked of them:
One who is working on this vine,
what is the law? May he eat from another vine?

phrases.aramaic: מִמִּין שֶׁאַתָּה נוֹתֵן לְכֵלָיו שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת בָּעֵינַן
phrases.english: Do we require that it be from the type that you put into the owner's vessels,
phrases.notes: This echoes the פסוק in דברים 23:25: the worker eats from the produce that goes into the owner's vessels.

phrases.english: and that is present here?
Or perhaps we require that it be from the very thing that you put
into the owner's vessels,
and that is not present here?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ עוֹשֶׂה בְּגֶפֶן זֶה מַהוּ שֶׁיֹּאכַל בְּגֶפֶן אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes the משנה's figs-and-grapes rule into a closer case: two vines of the same produce.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a worker's eating right limited to the same type of produce, or to the exact produce he is handling for the owner?

steps.title: If so, how can an ox ever eat from growing produce?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a difficulty for the strict side. If a worker may only eat from the exact vine he works on, how can an ox working on produce still attached to the ground ever eat?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that one working on this vine may not eat from another vine, then an ox working with attached produce, how does it eat?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the strict answer to the question. It asks how that answer could work for an ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה lets a working ox eat. But an ox working on growing produce usually is not standing right at the exact plant being worked on. If only that exact plant counts, it seems the ox could never eat.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you conclude to say

phrases.english: And if you conclude to say
that one who is working on this vine
may not eat from another vine,
then an ox working with attached produce, how does it eat?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּמְצֵי לוֹמַר עוֹשֶׂה בְּגֶפֶן זֶה לֹא יֹאכַל בְּגֶפֶן אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the strict side of the question and tests it against the case of an ox.
steps.kashyaTarget: The strict view that eating is allowed only from the exact produce being worked on.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under that view, an ox working on growing produce would almost never be able to eat, which seems impossible.

steps.title: The ox can eat from a long branch
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי answers that the ox can eat when the vine has long branches.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא son of רב אידי said: with long branches.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי answers the difficulty. He shows a case where the strict view still lets the ox eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a vine has a long branch, the ox can work at one part of the branch and eat from another part of that same branch. So the strict view does not make the ox's right impossible. The original question is still not decided.
steps.confusionAlert: This answer only shows that the strict view could work. It does not decide the question of whether a worker may eat from another vine.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, said:
With long branches.
phrases.notes: Picture a long branch: the ox works at one end and eats from the other end of that same branch.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי בִּשְׁרָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the ox difficulty from the previous step.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a realistic case where the difficulty disappears.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under the strict view, a working ox on growing produce could never eat.
steps.terutzMaskana: With long branches, the ox works on one part of the branch and eats from another part of it, so the strict view still works.

steps.title: A proof from the figs-and-grapes rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to prove from the משנה that a worker may eat from a different vine of the same kind of fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if he was working on figs, he may not eat grapes. That means figs and figs, like the case of figs and grapes, he may eat. Now if you say a worker on this vine may not eat from another vine, how could you ever find such a case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the line from the משנה about figs and grapes to try to answer its question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only bans eating a different kind of fruit. That implies he may eat the same kind of fruit, even from a different tree, just as the figs and grapes are on different trees. If he could only eat from the exact vine he works on, the case of 'figs and figs' on two trees would never be allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: This implies; it shows what we learn from the wording
Similar to, the same setup as
How could you find such a case?

phrases.english: Come and hear: if he was working on figs
phrases.notes: This is the משנה we saw back in step 16.

phrases.english: he may not eat grapes.
This implies that figs and other figs,
set up like the figs and grapes, he may eat.
phrases.notes: Figs and grapes grow on different trees, so the 'figs and figs' case also means two different trees.

phrases.english: And if you say that one working on this vine
may not eat from another vine,
how can you find this case?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הָיָה עוֹשֶׂה בִּתְאֵנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the side question about the ox is settled, the גמרא goes back to the main question from step 18.
steps.raayaObject: That a worker may eat from a different vine of the same kind
steps.raayaSupportSource: The implied permission for 'figs and figs' in the משנה

steps.title: The case is a vine with long branches
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי pushes off the proof: the משנה can be talking about one long-branched vine.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא son of רב אידי said: it is talking about a vine with long branches.
steps.whatsHappening: The proof is pushed off. The 'figs and figs' case can happen on one single plant, so it does not have to mean two different vines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a long, hanging vine, the worker can harvest one end of a branch and eat from the other end. That is still the same vine. So the משנה's wording fits even the strict side, and nothing is proven.

keyTerms.meaning: A vine trained so that its branches hang down long

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same answer רב שישא gave in step 20 about the ox. Here the גמרא uses it again to answer a different proof.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, said:
With a hanging vine.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי: בְּמוּדְלֵית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 21 by explaining the case differently.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The case can be one long vine, so it does not have to mean two vines.

steps.title: A proof from waiting for better fruit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to prove the strict side from the משנה's rule that a worker may hold off until he reaches better fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: but he may hold himself back until he reaches the place of the good fruit, and then eat. If you say a worker on this vine may eat from another vine, let him just go, bring some, and eat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second line of the משנה, this time to prove the opposite side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he were allowed to eat from any vine, he would not need to wait until his work brings him to the good vines. He could just go and get the good fruit now. The fact that he must wait suggests he may only eat from the vine he is working on.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him go, bring, and eat

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע: אֲבָל מוֹנֵעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ
phrases.english: Come and hear: But he may hold himself back
until he reaches the place of the good fruit, and eat.
And if you say that one working on this vine
may eat from another vine,
let him go and bring and eat!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: אֲבָל מוֹנֵעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ עַד שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִמְקוֹם הַיָּפוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new proof, this time for the strict side.
steps.raayaObject: That a worker may not eat from a different vine
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's rule that he waits until he reaches the better fruit

steps.title: Waiting is about not stopping work, so the question is narrowed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that he must wait only so he does not stop working. It then narrows the real question to the case where his wife and children could bring him the fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the reason is that walking over would make him stop working. That part we never asked about. What we are asking about is where his wife and children are there. What is the rule?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof and explains what its question really was all along.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Of course the worker cannot leave his job to go eat elsewhere, because that wastes the owner's time. So the משנה's 'wait' proves nothing about other vines. The open question is when someone else, like his wife or children, brings him fruit from another vine without him stopping work.

keyTerms.meaning: We were not asking about this

steps.whyThisMatters: This sharpens the whole question from step 18. It is no longer about the worker walking away, only about whether fruit from another vine is allowed to him at all.

phrases.english: There, it is because of stopping work
we were not asking about that,
what we were asking about
is where his wife and children are there; what is the rule?
phrases.notes: They could bring him fruit from the other vine while he keeps working.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם מִשּׁוּם בִּיטּוּל מְלָאכָה לָא קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 23 and restates the question more narrowly.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from waiting for the good fruit
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The waiting is because of stopping work, not because other vines are forbidden.

steps.title: Quoting the rule about eating while walking
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה's line that workers may eat while walking between rows and coming back from the winepress.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: in all these cases they only allowed eating during work. But to protect the owner's interests, they said workers may eat while walking from row to row and when coming back from the winepress.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third line from the משנה. This is setting up the proof, which the next step explains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says eating while walking is allowed only because of the חכמים, to protect the owner from losing time. The next step will show what this tells us about eating from another vine.

keyTerms.meaning: Returning a loss to the owner; here, saving him lost work time
From one row to the next row

phrases.english: Come and hear: And in all of these, they said
phrases.notes: This is the משנה from step 17.

phrases.english: only at the time of work,
but because of returning a loss to the owners
they said: workers may eat
as they walk from row to row
and on their way back from the winepress.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: וְכוּלָּם לֹא אָמְרוּ אֶלָּא בִּשְׁעַת מְלָאכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new attempt to answer the narrowed question from step 24.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a worker may eat from a different vine
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's rule about eating while walking between rows

steps.title: Walking counts as work, so it must be about a different vine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the proof: walking counts as working, yet by Torah law he may not eat then. So the reason must be that he is not by his own vine.
steps.simpleTranslation: They assumed that walking counts as doing work. Even so, he may eat only because of protecting the owner, and by Torah law he may not eat. This shows that one working on this vine may not eat from another vine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out how the משנה from step 25 proves the strict side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If walking counts as work, the Torah should already let him eat. The only thing missing is that he is not standing at the vine he is working on. So the Torah must allow eating only from the exact vine he works on.

keyTerms.meaning: They assumed, the starting idea of the proof

steps.whatToRemember: Three proofs were tried. The first two were pushed off. The third, from eating while walking, seems to show that by Torah law a worker eats only from the vine he is working on.
steps.confusionAlert: The proof only works because of the starting idea that walking counts as working. If that idea is wrong, the proof falls apart.

phrases.english: They assumed that one walking is like one doing work,
and it is because of returning a loss to the owners
that he eats,
but by Torah law he does not eat.
So we see that one working on this vine
may not eat from another vine.

steps.triggerLanguage: סַבְרוּהָ מְהַלֵּךְ כְּעוֹשֶׂה מַעֲשֶׂה דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the proof quoted in step 25.
steps.raayaObject: That a worker may not eat from a different vine
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה needs the חכמים' rule to allow eating while walking, even though walking counts as work

steps.title: Walking is not counted as working
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off the proof from Step 26. Maybe a worker on one vine may eat from another vine. He cannot eat while walking only because walking does not count as work.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. I can tell you that one who works on this vine may eat from another vine. A worker who is walking is simply not considered to be doing work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from Step 26. It gives a different reason why the walking worker may not eat by Torah law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 26 assumed that walking counts as work. On that view, the only reason he cannot eat is that he is not at his own vine. Here the גמרא says walking is not work at all. That alone explains why the Torah does not let him eat, so the משנה proves nothing about 'another vine.'

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, I can tell you. A standard opening for a different way to read the source.
One who is walking, here between rows or back from the winepress
One who is actually doing work
Is considered like, is the same as
A different vine from the one he is working on

phrases.english: No, actually I can tell you:
one who works on this vine
may eat from another vine,
and one who is walking is not considered like one doing work.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, לְעוֹלָם אֵימָא לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in Step 26 by denying its assumption that walking counts as work.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the walking worker in its first version
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed walking counts as work. If walking is not work, there is a different reason he cannot eat, and the 'another vine' question stays open.
steps.whatToRemember: In the first version, the proof from the walking worker fails. Walking may simply not count as work, so nothing is learned about eating from another vine.

steps.title: Second version: the same משנה proves he may eat from another vine
steps.stepSummary: Some say the discussion went differently. The Sages started out assuming that walking is not work. From the reason the walking worker cannot eat, they inferred that a worker on one vine may eat from another vine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: they assumed that one who is walking is not considered like one doing work. That is why by Torah law he does not eat: because he is not doing work. But one who is doing work does eat by Torah law. So it seems that one who works on this vine may eat from another vine!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version (איכא דאמרי) of the discussion. In this version, the walking-worker משנה is used to prove the lenient side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the starting assumption is that walking is not work. So the only reason the walking worker cannot eat is that he is not working. That suggests a worker who is working may eat, even from a vine he is not working on. The walking worker is not at his own vine either, and his only problem is that he is not working.

keyTerms.meaning: They assumed it. This is the starting assumption of the Sages in the discussion.
But this one. It points to the opposite case, which is learned by inference.
Apparently, so we see. It introduces the conclusion of a proof.

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the direction flip. In the first version (Steps 26–27), the walking-worker משנה was used to prove the strict side. In this second version, the same משנה is used to prove the lenient side: he may eat from another vine.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
they assumed that one who is walking
is not considered like one doing work.
And this is the reason
that by Torah law he does not eat:
because he is not considered like one doing work.
But one who is doing work
eats by Torah law,
phrases.notes: Even though the walking worker isn't standing at the vine he works on, the only thing holding him back is that he isn't working.

phrases.english: so apparently, one who works on this vine
may eat from another vine!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי סַבְרוּהָ מְהַלֵּךְ לָאו כְּעוֹשֶׂה מַעֲשֶׂה דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second version of the discussion of the same משנה (Step 25). It uses the assumption that Step 27 used to reject the first proof, and turns it into a proof for the lenient side.
steps.raayaObject: That a worker who is working on one vine may eat from a different vine
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about workers eating while walking between rows, read as saying the only problem with walking is that he is not working
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the same source can be read in two opposite directions. Everything depends on one starting assumption: whether walking counts as work.

steps.title: Rejecting the second proof: he may not eat from another vine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to push off the second version's proof. Maybe a worker on one vine really may not eat from another vine. The explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. I can tell you that one who works on this vine may not eat from another vine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to reject the proof from Step 28. This line sets up the rejection. The reason that explains the walking-worker משנה comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא holds on to the strict view that working on one vine does not allow eating from another. To defend it, it will have to explain the walking-worker משנה some other way. That explanation comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: No. It signals that the proof is being rejected.
One who works on this vine

phrases.english: No. Actually I can tell you:
one who works on this vine
may not eat from another vine,
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud, where the גמרא explains how the walking-worker משנה still fits this strict view.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא. לְעוֹלָם אֵימָא לָךְ: עוֹשֶׂה בְּגֶפֶן זֶה אֵינוֹ אוֹכֵל בְּגֶפֶן אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins rejecting the lenient proof of Step 28 by restating the strict view. The explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The second version's proof that a worker may eat from another vine
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Not yet spelled out here. The גמרא first states the strict view, and its explanation of the משנה comes on the next amud.
